source_evidence.claim: The source reports long-run black-cell densities for rules 126, 22, 30, 150, 182, and conditionally 110, and points to page 953 for an estimation method.

The same rules have stated long-run local-pattern properties: rules 30 and 150 retain random-looking rows, rule 126 favors black pairs, rule 182 surrounds white cells by black, and rule 22 has four-cell conditions.
Triangle densities of size n decay roughly as 2^-n for rules 126, 30, 150, and 182 and roughly as 1.3^-n for rule 22.

For the source's special randomness-producing rule-22 seeds, the evolved pattern has density about 0.35, its center is never black on two successive steps, white follows white about twice as often as black follows white, and repetitive regions occur on both sides of the random middle.

source_evidence.claim: Generalized additivity combines evolution histories using an operation ⊕.
Generalized additivity requires phi[u⊕v] == phi[u]⊕phi[v].
The property is a homomorphism condition and ordinary Mod[u+v,k] supplies the modular-addition example, coinciding with Xor only for k=2.
Rule 250 supplies the Max/Or generalized-additive variant.

Any initial-condition history can be reconstructed under ⊕ by combining Green-function histories from basic initial conditions; the familiar construction requires ⊕ to be associative, commutative, and to have an identity, making a commutative monoid.
The source enumerates counts of inequivalent commutative monoids by color count k.
The source tabulates numbers of rules additive over each commutative monoid for stated k and r cases.
Every such local rule applies monoid endomorphisms sigma to neighborhood cells and combines the results with ⊕.

The basic local rules have the form RotateLeft[a] ⊕ RotateRight[a]; endomorphisms sigma act as position weights, multi-cell rules combine repeated flattened instances of ⊕, and the resulting associative-rule patterns are at most nested.

source_evidence.claim: Assuming independent cell colors at density p gives product probabilities for every neighborhood.
The code constructs the eight three-cell neighborhood probabilities as products of p and 1-p.
The next density is obtained by weighting the rule table with those neighborhood probabilities.
The next density is probs . IntegerDigits[m,2,8].

Rule 22 gives one-step map 3p(1-p)^2 with nonzero stable estimate 1-1/Sqrt[3] approximately 0.42 versus actual density 0.35095; the two-step map p(1-p)^2(2+3p^2) yields 0.35012, and the three-step map p(1-p)^2(p^4-18p^3+41p^2-22p+6) yields 0.379.
The one-step mean-field maps for rules 90 and 30 are respectively 2p(1-p) and p(2p^2-5p+3), and both imply final density 1/2.
The approximation scheme is also called mean field theory and is stated to tend to work better in higher dimensions.
Probabilistic estimates can also target difference-pattern growth rates, but correlation buildup usually prevents systematic improvement of such approximations.
